subject: pixelDungeonProps
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: dungeon props: chest, torches, barrels, bones, spike trap.
Style: pixel art.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module that builds a dungeon prop group using the SDK and pixel kit, covering chest, torches, barrels, bones, and a spike trap. Since the builder requires exactly one root joint, I'll create a plain "root" joint at the origin and attach all prop parts to it since props don't need their own joint hierarchy.

I'm sketching dimensions and layout: a chest around 0.9 wide sitting center-back, standing torches on stone bases roughly 1.4m tall with glowing flames, and barrels sized like real 0.6m diameter casks arranged nearby, all positioned relative to the chest at the origin.

For the pixel aesthetic, I'm using blocky tileBox geometry for straight-edged props and lathe shapes with cellPaint for cylindrical ones like barrels, giving an octagonal profile so the voxel-style texture mapping snaps cleanly to each face. I'm also planning a spike trap floor plate in front of the chest and scattering bones like skulls and ribs nearby for detail, keeping the whole scene within about 4 meters wide and centered on x=0.

Working out the barrel's radius profile with a bulge in the middle and quantizing the radius values into discrete pixel-like steps, then adding separate iron hoop rings as thin lathe bands slightly larger than the barrel surface at matching heights for the banded silhouette look.

Finishing the lathe profile and checking it closes cleanly without self-crossing, then setting segment count and rotation offset for the spin.

For the barrel's wood texture, I'm working out plank widths relative to octagon face circumference so seams land naturally, accounting for how diagonal faces get slightly irregular cell shapes.

Picking a brown wood color ramp and varying shading by noise and vertical position, then thinking about adding lid-specific ring patterns radiating from each barrel's center, which means wrapping the paint logic in a function that takes the barrel's position and seed so each instance gets consistent but varied texture.

Now I'm working out hoop placement — four iron rings positioned at set height fractions, each defined as a thin outlined band whose inner and outer radius is derived from the barrel's stepped profile so the hoop sits snug against the wood surface. I'm also planning barrel variants: an intact standing one, an open-topped one showing dark contents, and a barrel lying on its side using a rotated lathe shape with a horizontal axis.

For the lying barrel, I'm figuring out how to shift the base position along the axis so it rests properly, generalizing the barrel-building function to accept a base position and axis vector, and using the dot product between surface normal and axis direction to detect which face is the lid for coloring purposes.

For an open barrel variant, I'm designing a recessed top profile that reveals interior walls, then considering adding a murky disc near the top to suggest water or slime inside. Now I'm starting on the chest shape, sketching out box dimensions for the body.

For the chest lid, I'm working out a stepped profile extruded along the depth, using columns of varying heights to approximate a rounded top shape...

Working out the extrusion for the lid, centering it along the correct axis, then figuring out how plank seam textures should map to each face depending on which direction the planks run.

I'm leaning toward using cellPaint consistently across the extrude and box shapes for the planks, reserving tileBox or pixel-art textures just for small details like the lock plate, emblem, skull, and coin. I'm also roughing out the paint budget—estimating total painted surface area against the texel density needed for a 1024 paint sheet.

Given the estimated surface area (barrels, chest, torches, trap, bones totaling around 13 m²), I'm bumping up to a 2048 paint sheet for crisper texels even though 1024 would technically work. Now I'm sketching the chest's iron bands as slightly oversized boxes running vertically at fixed x-offsets across the lid.

Still writing lid band geometry...

Now I'm planning the chest corner posts as iron brackets positioned at the four corners.

For the lock, I'll add a protruding box on the front face with a gold lock-and-keyhole texture sized to show a small pixel drawing.

Now I'm thinking about whether the chest should be open or closed—an open lid revealing treasure looks more appealing, so I'll model the lid as a hinged joint at the back-top edge, rotated back roughly 100 degrees, using the joint's local axis to control the hinge rotation.

Since lid parts built before posing inherit the rotation correctly, I'll build the lid pieces first, then apply the pose so they land open. For the chest body, I'll construct it as open-topped—four walls plus a floor—so a coin pile sitting near the top surface is visible inside.

Adding a smaller step mound above that, plus scattered gems and flat coin cylinders with a subtle glow on a few pieces. I'll keep the lid open with matching dark wood lining on its underside.

I'm setting up the joint hierarchy with a single root joint and a hinge joint for the lid, plus a helper function for creating boxes attached to specific bones so part placement stays unambiguous.

For the trap, I'll add a slider-style joint for the raised spikes parented to root. For the torch, I'm designing a stepped stone base, a thin wooden pole, an iron bracket, a charred cloth wrap for the head, and a pixelated glowing flame built from stacked colored boxes in orange, yellow, and white to mimic a flickering glow.

Writing flame geometry...

I'll use flat colors for the glow materials and skip actual lights since there aren't any in the model. For variety I'm adding a second torch that's fallen over near the barrels—a charred, extinguished pole lying along the X axis with a few dim embers still glowing instead of a full flame.

For the stone base I'm painting a gray ramp with cobble-style seams using randomized blocks for texture variety. The spike trap gets a slab floor with a framed pit, a grid of small pyramid-cone spikes in iron paint, plus rust and blood-stain decals, cracked tile patterns, and maybe one skewed spike for detail.

Now I'm building the pit recess from four boxes forming a frame with a dark floor plate beneath, then raising the spikes up through it with an iron base plate underneath, and adding a textured blood-stain plane on the frame edge along with red paint accents on some spike tips.

For the spikes themselves, I'm weighing a rotated pyramidal cone shape versus a stepped pixel-style version made from stacked boxes of decreasing width, leaning toward the stacked boxes for a more blocky, pixel-art look.

For the skull, I'm planning a voxel build using separate boxes for the cranium and jaw, with eye sockets suggested through a small pixel-art texture mapped onto the front face.

Deciding on the full skeleton kit: two skulls, three femurs, and a ribcage built from vertebrae boxes plus curved rib tubes swept along arcs with a square cross-section, keeping the paint texel smaller (0.01) for these thinner bone pieces to preserve detail.

Now I'm sketching the scene layout: a chest at center, two upright barrels and one lying barrel positioned to the left and right with slightly offset coordinates, torches flanking the group near x=±2, and a bone pile placed front-left with a few scattered small bones near the treasure.

Torches at 1.6m feel right for real-world scale. For textures, I'm planning pixel-art details like a lock, skull decal, runes etched on the trap plate, a danger emblem, stains, and a branded mark on the barrel for extra grime and character.

Paint categories cover wood, barrel wood, stone, iron, gold, bone, pit shadows, torch poles, and cloth wraps. Given how much code this involves, I'll keep things organized with helper functions and write carefully to avoid API mistakes.

Now I'm setting up imports from the builder SDK, defining a texel constant and metadata, and initializing the builder with a root joint at the origin. I'm also writing a box helper function that wraps the builder's part creation with geometry, color, position, and options.

Writing wood palette seam logic...

I'm fixing the modulo to handle negatives properly, then mapping plank/stave coordinates per face: chest planks use y for front/side faces and z for the top, while barrel staves need to pick the right axis (u or v) depending on orientation and handle the seam direction for lying versus standing barrels.

For the lying barrel I'm realizing the seams need to follow the angle around the cylinder's axis rather than a flat coordinate, so I'm computing stave index from the angle between two perpendicular vectors at each cell center, though I need to be careful since seam detection only works at cell granularity.

Rather than trying to detect neighbor differences I'll mark a cell as a seam when its fractional stave position falls below a small threshold, giving stave widths of roughly 4-5 cells near the typical radius - not perfectly uniform but visually fine at this resolution. This same angle-based approach should work for the standing barrel orientation too.

For octagon barrels the flat-side geometry still works fine with this angle method, and lid rims can get a darker ring near the edge based on radial distance from center. I'm setting up a local coordinate frame (two perpendicular vectors spanning the plane orthogonal to the barrel's axis) so I can compute angle and height for any point relative to an arbitrary barrel orientation.

To keep texel evaluation fast across millions of samples, I'm avoiding Vector3 allocations and just working with raw numbers for the dot products and distances. Now I'm sketching the barrel-building function itself, including a radius profile that varies along height to give it that classic barrel bulge shape.

Building outline points...

For each hoop segment I'm lathing a rectangular outline between inner and outer radius across the y-range, using 8 segments with a 22.5° spin so the octagon faces align consistently, accounting for apothem versus vertex radius.

For the barrel lying horizontally, I'm figuring out the resting position so the octagon's flat face sits at the bottom, which means working out whether the vertex radius or the apothem determines where the surface touches y=0 given the 22.5° spin offset in the lathe's local frame.

I'm positioning the barrel's base at a tilted axis for horizontal lying, and adding slime contents as a small glowing green disc near the top opening for the open/standing barrel variant.

I'm now working out a brand decal for the barrel — a red flame or skull symbol projected onto the front face, applied only to standing barrels since tilted orientations complicate the directional projection.

For stone textures, I'm designing a brick/flagstone pattern using cell coordinates to create staggered rows with seams, keeping the logic simple with periodic offsets per row to fake mortar lines.

I'm setting up a dithered blue-gray color ramp for brick shading and writing a deterministic hash function (using multiplication constants and bit operations) so each brick gets a consistent pseudo-random shade based on its position and seed, rather than varying per individual cell.

Adding more material ramps...

Still shaping the torch pole and bands...

Layering flame colors with crossed extrudes to build depth: outer orange, mid lighter orange, and bright yellow core, each slightly thicker so edges peek out and create a glowing layered look.

Close enough, that's fine. Now I'm designing the flame outline shape row by row with asymmetric half-widths to create a flickering, tapered tip effect, stepping the cells upward through height 10.

I'm extruding the outline along a staircase path with flat color materials, keeping the color palette manageable. For the fallen torch, I'm planning a pole lying sideways with a charred wrapped end and a few scattered glowing embers nearby.

Writing rotation helper function...

For the skull, I'm thinking of building it as a sheet with cranium and jaw dimensions, keeping the jaw as a separate part so it reads as detachable even without a hinge. On the cranium face I'll stamp dithered eye sockets, a nose notch, and a crack, while the jaw gets alternating white/dark teeth rows, and maybe a small red or green glow pixel in one eye socket for character.

Now I'm deciding to keep just one texture sheet rather than separate glowing/non-glowing variants, embedding tiny glow boxes directly in the eye sockets of the pile skull. For construction, I'm defining a skull function that positions and rotates a skinned box for the cranium and a smaller skinned box for the jaw, offset below and in front of the cranium center.

I'm simplifying to two skulls using yaw-only rotation, skipping a side-rolled skull, with one perched on a raised bone pile. For the texture generation, I'm writing the pixel-fill logic that walks through each face rectangle and colors it using a bone-colored ramp with dithering based on a Bayer pattern.

Now I'm sketching the eye and nose placement on the cranium's front face, mapping out a row-by-row pixel pattern for the eye sockets and nose triangle within the stamped texture region.

Next I'm adding a forehead crack detail using the dark outline palette, then moving to the jaw piece's pixel layout with alternating teeth and gap colors.

Then I'm planning the chest ornaments as flat-colored gems—ruby red, sapphire blue, emerald green—before moving on to designing a spike trap texture.

Now I'm working out the rune carvings on the trap's stone frame, placing glyph tiles at the corners and defining the frame geometry around a pit: outer slab dimensions, frame segments on each side, and the inner pit cutout proportions.

Then I'm designing the pit floor as a dark iron box set slightly recessed, with a spike plate above it, and building the spikes themselves as stepped pyramid shapes using a lathe profile with decreasing radii at each height segment.

For varied spike heights, I'm planning to vary the step count per spike (3 to 5 steps) across a 4×4 grid, so some spikes appear shorter or broken by truncating the profile early with a flat top instead of a sharp point.

Now I'm adding iron paint to the spikes with blood-red accents near the tips using noise-based blending, plus a lighter highlight at the very top, and setting up the spike joint attached to a base plate so it can be posed.

For the frame corners, I'm placing four rune-textured planes facing upward, making sure their orientation vectors don't degenerate by giving them a custom up direction so the glowing symbols render correctly.

I want the rune tinted red-orange with a glow effect so it reads as a magical sigil against the stone, using a transparent background so only the glyph itself shows through. I'm sketching a small 9x9 pixel star-like design with two warm colors, red for the outer points and amber for the center, sized to fit the 0.12 plane.

For the overall texture set, I'm deciding I don't need a separate blood-stain texture since I can fake that with paint directly on the trap spikes or pit floor. That leaves me with roughly five core textures—lock plate, skull, brand mark, rune, and a chest emblem—which fits comfortably within the target range of five to twelve.

Adding a second brand variant with crossbones for the other barrel brings the texture count to six. Now I'm placing scattered gold coins as flat cylinder discs with random tilts across the top of a treasure mound, sized and colored to catch a warm glow, positioned on a raised base layer near the top of the pile.

I'm also working out the chest's interior dimensions—wall thickness, floor thickness, and the coin layer's bounding box so it sits properly inside the walls without clipping.

Now I'm positioning the four wall panels (front, back, left, right) around the chest's center, then setting up the lid as a hinged piece attached at the back edge, extruded with its own banding details.

Next I'm adding hardware: corner plates, a hasp box on the lid's front face, and a matching lock plate on the body front, working out their exact positions and sizes relative to the lid's height.

Now I'm checking whether the lid collides with anything when opened 100° about the back hinge, tracing how the lid's local "up" axis rotates to point backward and downward as it swings open.

Checking that the open bottom face of the lid extrusion correctly rotates to face front, confirming the orientation works. I'm adding a thin red cloth lining box just inside the lid's bottom to represent interior fabric.

Setting lining center z=0, confirming geometry lines up with the hinge point. Now defining the lid's hinge joint, anchoring it at the chest's edge with a rotation axis along z, and positioning it relative to the chest's offset.

Working out chest-relative coordinates for the other props now, simplifying by placing the chest at the origin and arranging torches, barrels, and the lying barrel around it -- checking spacing so the torches at ±2.1 don't collide with nearby barrels, nudging them out to ±2.3, and figuring out the lying barrel's axis orientation and z-span based on its length and tilt.

Now checking the spike trap, bones, and fallen torch positions against the chest and lying barrel so nothing overlaps, keeping total scene extents around 5m wide by 1.7m tall, with a slight flicker-seed variation planned for the second torch.

For the skeletal remains, I'm planning femur bones as simple shaft boxes with lumpy end knobs built from small split boxes, and considering whether the ribcage should lie flat as a semicircular arc sweep or stand as half-buried hoops like a skeleton resting on its back.

Still building the ribcage geometry... pairs of rib arcs curving from a spine line, each swept along a catmull path with a small polygonal cross-section, tapering toward the ends, plus boxy vertebrae segments spaced along the spine.

Now I'm positioning two skulls — one beside the ribcage, and another resting on the front edge of the trapezoid frame, figuring out the y-height so it sits properly on the surface and centering it along that front edge.

I'm settling on the skull's rotation so it faces toward the viewer rather than away, landing on roughly a -20 to 25 degree yaw. Then I add scattered tiny bone fragments, iron bracket details on the torch, cracked stone base texture, and moss patches, and start estimating the overall part count for the chest and bars.

Tallying the full scene part count across barrels, torches, the trap mechanism, and bone scatter brings me to roughly 190 parts, comfortably under budget, with triangle counts fine too. I confirm the flat color palette stays under the limit while paint operations remain unrestricted.

Setting up imports...

Writing hash and modulo helper functions...

Defining the stone surface paint function...

Adding moss patches and iron paint variant...

Adding ember-orange speckles for the lit torch head and defining a darker walnut wood ramp with a red tint for the chest.

Now I'm picking a honey-toned barrel palette and a muted pole palette, then writing a barrelPaint function that builds an orthonormal basis around the barrel's axis to apply procedural staining.

Still writing barrel shading logic...

For caps I'll check if the normal is strongly axis-aligned to detect the recess floor, applying dark there too, and I'll use dithered ramp picking for the seam shading. Now I'm starting to write the barrel generator function itself.

Writing barrel function...

Still writing hoop geometry logic...

Now I'm working out the brand decal placement, positioning it near the surface of the body using an offset based on the brand direction and side coordinates.

Writing body construction code...

I realize a solid band box would hide the coins inside when the lid opens, so instead I need to make the iron bands thin surface strips on the front, back, and top faces only, rather than filling the interior.

Still placing bands and corner brackets...

Now I'm designing the lock plate, a small pixel-art texture box on the front with a bordered outline pattern.

Still mapping out keyhole pixel grid...

Expanding to 10 rows and now sketching the lid geometry—bands, hasp, outline shape, and extrusion parameters for the chest's top piece.

Now I'm placing the hasp, a small iron box attached to the lid's front face, working out its position relative to the last column's z-span so it sits flush against the front edge.

I'm also checking the lid's rotation joint: with axis [1,0,0], positive degrees should tip the lid forward and down as expected, confirming the -100 degree open rotation makes sense. I'm now defining the lid joint's parent, position, and direction attachment.

Now I'm writing the torch-building function, stacking base boxes of decreasing size, adding a pole with iron bands at set heights, and topping it with a cup and prongs to hold the flame -- working out the exact heights and centers for each piece.

I'm adding glowing embers around the flame and considering whether the torch head needs more height, then moving on to designing a fallen-torch variant with a rotated pole, charred wrap, and iron cup placed via a positioning function.

For the spike trap, I'm setting up rune plane geometry textured and glowing, placed with directional orientation. For the pit floor, I'm using a flat dark color and thinking about adding blood stain patches as painted details.

For trap frames, I'm setting stone paint and slab heights with an iron spike plate. Now I'm sketching a skull-building function that positions a cranium and jaw mesh relative to a frame orientation, working out the vertical offsets so the cranium center sits above the jaw and the jaw nests slightly forward and overlapping the cranium's bottom edge.

I'm figuring out the glow-eye socket placement, working through the viewer's perspective versus world coordinates to map pixel positions on the cranium face to the correct x-axis direction given the model faces +z and the viewer looks toward -z.

I'll place the glow plate slightly in front of the face at z=+0.102, sized small to sit right over the socket, and apply the skull's yaw rotation to the whole group.

For the femur, I'm writing a helper that builds a shaft box plus rounded knob boxes at each end, using the frame's position and rotation to orient it along the limb direction. Now I'm moving on to building the ribcage.

For the ribcage, I'm placing seven spine vertebrae boxes spaced along the z-axis, then generating curved rib paths on each side using Catmull-Rom splines through widening points, and sweeping a small bone-colored cross-section along those paths to form the ribs.

Next I'm scattering 16 coins randomly within a bounded x/z area near the top, using a seeded random generator for consistent placement.

I'll place the ruby gem on the mound with a strong glow effect, then verify the `b.part` function signature works correctly with bone and position options for placing geometry. I should also check how decals get applied to targets.

Designing brand textures as pixel-grid icons...

Finishing that skull glyph grid, checking row widths match at 9 columns each, then setting decal size and palette colors. Barrel A gets BRAND2, barrel B gets BRAND_X at a different yaw rotation, while barrel C stays plain.

I'm settling on five textures total: LOCK, SKULL, RUNE, BRAND_X, BRAND_SKULL, deciding against extra additions like a crest emblem or coin texture to keep things manageable. I list out the glow elements I need: flames, embers, runes, gems, coins, skull eyes, and slime, then move to writing the builder setup with proper options for naming and paint size, and start thinking about floor contact handling for the props.

Writing box helper and plank paint logic...

Writing barrel paint function...

Still defining recess shading logic...

For an octagon, radius varies between the apothem (0.92R) and the vertex radius (R) depending on angle, so the outer wall spans roughly [0.23, 0.25] and the inner wall spans [0.198, 0.215] — putting the threshold around 0.222 to separate them cleanly.

Simplifying the cap logic: I'll detect plank boundaries using a modulo index on the angular coordinate to create seams every 4 units, then derive the plank index from that same counter for the rim geometry.

For the wall I'm computing stave boundaries by dividing the angle into 20 equal segments, finding the fractional position within each stave to detect seam gaps, and using the floored stave number to drive per-stave shading variation.

Now I'm adding wear and grime: darkening the base where height is low to simulate ground contact, plus noise-based dark stains for mud, and painting the hoop cells with iron color. For the trap/spike detail, I'm defining a joint at the target position, then lathing a four-sided spike shape with a slight spin and assigning it the spike paint color and bone.

I'm varying spike heights per position using a hash function, marking a couple as broken stubs, and painting blood-red tips on taller spikes based on height and noise thresholds, using a dark blood color ramp. I'm also finalizing the layering: the pit floor sits lowest, the plate above it, the spikes rising from the plate, and the frame top just above the spike bases, so the trap reads correctly as a pit with spikes recessed below the frame.

Now I'm placing the torches and barrels around the central chest, computing each standing barrel's base position, axis, seed, and brand direction, plus working out the lying barrel's center and axis so I can derive its base point and orient its hoops and staves consistently with the same painting function. I'm also considering knocking the cap off the lying barrel for variety.

I'm deciding to make barrel C an open lying barrel with its recessed end facing the viewer, adding a glowing green slime disc inside barrel B's open top, sized and positioned to sit just below the rim with octagonal rotation to match the staves, and checking the hoop placement fractions still clear the recess. Writing torch paint function...

Still writing extrude logic...

Generating skull texture layout...

Still mapping pixel details for the eyes and cracks, then moving on to define the jaw face layout next.

Defining the rib positions and widths...

I need to confirm the lid pose happens after its parts are built, and that the decal target surface references the barrel mesh correctly in model space. With those checks done, I'm ready to finalize the description and verify the flame glow color strings are distinct.
